prompt: Write a warm but professional welcome message for a new remote employee's first day, to be posted in the team channel. Under 90 words. Must mention their name "Dana", their role "backend engineer", and name one specific person to go to with questions. No more than one exclamation mark. Do not use "excited".

constraints.text: Mentions the backend engineer role and one named go-to person
At most one exclamation mark; warm but professional

prompt: Write the agenda email for a difficult meeting: telling a vendor their contract won't be renewed. Under 110 words. Subject line required, formatted as "Subject: ..." on the first line. Do not reveal the non-renewal decision in the email itself — frame it as a contract review. No pleasantries beyond one opening line.

constraints.text: Decision is not revealed; framed as contract review

prompt: Write a press-release opening paragraph for a small town library reopening after flood repairs, 18 months later. One paragraph, 60-90 words. Include the reopening date "March 14" and one detail about what's new. Quote the head librarian, "R. Alvarez", exactly once. No superlatives ("best", "greatest", "state-of-the-art").

constraints.text: Exactly one quotation from the librarian; no superlatives
Includes one concrete new feature detail

prompt: Write feedback for a direct report whose written reports are excellent but who goes silent in meetings. Structure as exactly 2 paragraphs under 130 words: first the strength (be specific), then the growth area with one concrete, low-stakes first step. Do not use the words "shy", "quiet", or "confidence". End with an offer of support, one sentence.

constraints.text: Strength is specific; growth step is concrete and low-stakes
Ends with a one-sentence support offer

prompt: Write the FAQ answer for "Can I get a refund?" for a small online course business. Policy: full refund within 14 days if less than 20% of the course is completed; nothing after. Under 100 words. State both conditions precisely. Include one empathetic line without groveling. Do not use the word "unfortunately" or "policy".

constraints.text: Both conditions (14 days AND <20% completed) stated precisely

prompt: Explain to a skeptical grandparent why their grandchild's "YouTuber" ambition is a real (if risky) career path. Exactly 3 paragraphs under 160 words: what the job actually involves, the honest odds and downside, what a sensible version of pursuing it looks like. No hype words: "influencer" and "content creator" are banned. Stay respectful of the grandparent's skepticism.

constraints.text: Honest about odds/downside; describes a sensible pursuit path
Tone respects the skeptic rather than dismissing them

prompt: Why does traffic sometimes jam on a highway with no accident or construction? Explain the phantom jam to a commuter in exactly 2 paragraphs under 140 words, using a wave or ripple analogy. Include one thing an individual driver can do that measurably helps. Do not use the words "shockwave" or "equilibrium".

constraints.text: Names one individually-actionable helpful behavior (e.g. steady speed, bigger gap)

prompt: A friend asks why you shouldn't charge your phone to 100% every night. Give the honest, nuance-preserving answer in under 130 words, exactly 2 paragraphs: the battery-chemistry gist without jargon (the words "lithium", "cathode", and "electrolyte" are banned), then how much it actually matters in practice and when to ignore the advice. End by saying what you personally would do, one sentence.

constraints.text: Explains high-charge stress without the banned jargon
Quantifies practical impact honestly (small; convenience may win)
Ends with a one-sentence personal recommendation

prompt: Explain to a new juror what "beyond a reasonable doubt" means, in exactly 3 paragraphs under 150 words: what it is, what it is not (contrast with the civil standard), and one concrete way to think about doubt during deliberation. Do not use percentages or numbers to define the standard. The phrase "reasonable doubt" must appear.

constraints.text: No numeric/percentage definition of the standard
Contrasts with the civil preponderance standard
Legal content is accurate at lay level

prompt: Answer in valid JSON only with keys "myth", "reality", "origin": address the claim "we only use 10% of our brains". "myth" restates the claim in one sentence, "reality" corrects it in under 40 words, "origin" explains where the myth may have come from in under 30 words. No text outside the JSON.

constraints.text: Reality correction is accurate (whole brain is active; imaging shows this)

prompt: Our 4-person book club keeps dying because nobody finishes the book. Redesign it as exactly 4 numbered rules that lower the effort floor. One rule must make partial reading legitimate. One rule must cap meeting length with a stated number of minutes. Under 120 words. Do not suggest changing to audiobooks.

constraints.text: One rule legitimizes partial reading; one caps minutes with a number
Rules genuinely lower the effort floor (not just exhortations)

prompt: Plan the first 30 minutes after discovering a burst pipe under the kitchen sink, as exactly 5 numbered steps in strict priority order. Step 1 must be shutting off water with where to find the valve. One step must be about documentation for insurance. Under 130 words. No step may assume tools beyond a phone and towels.

constraints.text: Step 1 is water shutoff; one step covers insurance documentation
No tools assumed beyond phone and towels

prompt: A college freshman has $120/month for food beyond their meal plan's 10 dinners. Build a weekly eating strategy as exactly 4 bullet points (using "-"): how to stretch the 10 dinners, a $/week grocery target with arithmetic, two cheap-protein staples by name, and the one habit that wrecks this budget. Under 130 words.

constraints.text: Names two specific cheap proteins; names one budget-wrecking habit

prompt: Design a fair process for 3 siblings to divide their late parent's non-valuable but sentimental belongings. Exactly 5 numbered steps. One step must handle two people wanting the same item, without money changing hands. One step must set a pace (sessions, not one marathon). Under 150 words. The words "auction" and "lottery" must not appear.

constraints.text: Pacing step spreads the process over sessions
Process is genuinely fair (rotation/turn order addressed)

prompt: I inherited a 20-year-old car with 90K miles that runs fine. Keep it or sell it and lease something new? Give me a decision plan (not the decision) as exactly 4 numbered steps: what to inspect (with cost), what number to compare against what, the tipping-point question, and a revisit schedule. Under 140 words. Do not recommend either option.

constraints.text: Contains "90K" or engages the car's specifics
Genuinely neutral: no recommendation leaks through
Comparison step names concrete numbers to compare

prompt: A designer handed us a 14MB hero image for the homepage. Explain what to do instead, as exactly 3 numbered steps (convert/compress, size variants, lazy-load or CDN), each with the tool-agnostic principle and rough size target. Under 140 words. Include one number for an acceptable hero image size. Do not name any specific software product or service.

constraints.text: Gives a numeric acceptable size target (e.g. under ~300KB)
No specific products named; principles are correct

prompt: Someone on the team wants to add a 15th configuration option to our internal tool. Argue the hidden cost of configuration options in exactly 2 paragraphs under 140 words, including the testing-combinations math for 15 boolean flags stated as a number (2^15 = 32768). Then a final single-sentence paragraph proposing what to do with the request instead. Do not use "bloat".

constraints.text: Final paragraph is one sentence proposing an alternative (default, remove, usage data)
The combinatorial-testing argument is presented correctly (not just asserted)

prompt: Write the deprecation notice for an internal API endpoint /v1/reports, replaced by /v2/reports, sunset in 90 days. Format: exactly these headers in order: "## What changes", "## Timeline", "## Migration". Under 130 words. Include one breaking difference between v1 and v2 (invent something plausible) and a code-free migration step list of exactly 3 bullets under the Migration header.

constraints.text: Has the three required headers in order
Migration bullets are actionable and code-free

prompt: Explain race conditions using only a shared kitchen analogy (two roommates, one fridge) — no code, no computing vocabulary: the words "thread", "process", "lock", and "mutex" are banned. Exactly 2 paragraphs under 140 words. The second paragraph must map the kitchen fix back to "what software does" in one general sentence at the end.

constraints.text: Ends with one general mapping sentence

prompt: Answer in valid JSON only with keys "keep", "toss", "why": we have 3 years of application logs costing $800/month in storage; legal needs 12 months retained. "keep" states what to retain and where (one sentence), "toss" what to delete or downgrade (one sentence), "why" the one-sentence principle. No text outside the JSON.

constraints.text: Suggests tiering/cold storage rather than only deletion

prompt: A city proposes free downtown parking on weekends to help local shops. Steelman it, then break it: exactly these headers in order: "## The case", "## The catch", "## Better lever". Under 160 words. The catch must include what happens to spot turnover. The better lever must be one specific alternative policy. Do not use the word "induced".

constraints.text: Has the three required headers in order
Covers turnover (free spots fill with all-day parkers)
Steelman is genuine; alternative policy is specific

prompt: Two candidates for one barista job: A has 5 years experience but availability conflicts with your busiest shift; B has zero experience but full availability and great references from a fast-paced retail job. Recommend one in exactly 2 paragraphs under 140 words: compare against what the role actually needs, then commit with the single decisive factor named. Do not propose hiring both or splitting shifts.

constraints.text: Commits to one candidate with a named decisive factor
Analysis is grounded in the role's actual needs (coverage, trainability)

prompt: Our app's daily active users doubled after we added streaks, but support tickets about "lost streaks" now top the queue and app-store reviews mention "stressful". Assess whether streaks were net positive in exactly 3 paragraphs under 170 words: the win, the cost (including which users bear it), and a keep/modify/remove verdict with one design change if you say modify. The word "engagement" may appear at most once.

constraints.text: Identifies who bears the cost; verdict commits (with design change if modify)

prompt: A relative wants to put their $15K emergency fund into a friend's restaurant for "guaranteed 20% returns". Without giving investment advice, lay out the questions they should ask, as exactly 5 bullet points (using "-"), each a single question. One must be about what "guaranteed" legally means here; one about what happens to the money if the restaurant closes. Under 110 words. Do not tell them to invest or not to invest.

constraints.text: Each bullet is exactly one question
No advice to invest or abstain anywhere

prompt: Evaluate this argument: "Remote work is over — our office badge swipes are back to 80% of 2019 levels." List what the badge data can and cannot show, using exactly these headers in order: "## What it shows", "## What it can't show", "## Verdict". Under 150 words. The verdict must be one sentence and must not fully accept or fully dismiss the claim.

constraints.text: Has the three required headers in order
Verdict is one sentence, neither full acceptance nor dismissal
Names concrete blind spots (days per person, who swipes, hybrid patterns)

prompt: Write an acceptance speech for "Employee of the Month" at a paperclip factory, delivered by someone who is visibly unsure why they won. Under 120 words, one paragraph. The speech must thank exactly two named coworkers. Play it straight — the humor comes from sincerity, not jokes. The word "paperclip" must appear at least twice.

constraints.text: "paperclip" appears at least twice; humor is played straight
The winner's confusion is present but understated

prompt: Write a weather forecast for an imaginary city where emotions fall as weather. Exactly 4 numbered items covering morning, afternoon, evening, and overnight, in that order. Each item names an emotion-weather (e.g. "scattered nostalgia") and gives practical advice in forecast register. Under 120 words. No real weather words: "rain", "snow", "sun", and "cloud" are banned.

constraints.text: Four time blocks in order; forecast register maintained
Emotion-weather inventions are evocative and consistent

prompt: Write the lost-and-found notice a dragon would post after misplacing its hoard. Under 110 words. Format: a title line in all caps, then one paragraph. Must include a reward offer and a description of exactly three specific lost items. The dragon must remain in denial about having burned down the storage barn itself. No dialogue.

constraints.text: Describes exactly three specific lost items
Title line in all caps, then a single paragraph
The barn-burning denial is present but never admitted

prompt: Write a villanelle-lite: a 9-line poem in three 3-line stanzas about doing laundry at 2am, where the first line of stanza one returns as the last line of stanza three, exactly repeated. The word "quiet" must appear. No rhyme requirements otherwise. The mood is peaceful, not lonely.

constraints.text: Three stanzas separated by blank lines
Opening line returns exactly as the final line
Mood lands as peaceful rather than lonely

prompt: Write the minutes of a secret meeting of neighborhood squirrels planning winter acorn logistics, in dry corporate-minutes style. Use exactly these headers in order: "## Attendees", "## Decisions", "## Action items". Under 130 words. Attendees must list exactly 4 squirrels with plausible squirrel names. One action item must reference "the dog incident" without explaining it.

constraints.text: Has the three required headers in order
Corporate-minutes register throughout; incident never explained
